lesson.title: Knowing That Other Minds Know Differently
lesson.summary: Theory of mind is the ability to understand that other people have beliefs, desires, and knowledge different from your own, and it develops gradually over early childhood.
lesson.body:
Theory of mind is the understanding that other people have mental states, beliefs, desires, intentions, and knowledge, that can be different from your own and that guide their behavior. It sounds obvious to an adult, but it is a genuine cognitive achievement. To predict what someone will do, you have to represent not the world as it actually is, but the world as that other person believes it to be, even when you know their belief is wrong.

This connects directly to egocentrism, the preoperational child's difficulty separating their own perspective from someone else's. A child who has not yet developed theory of mind is not being selfish or careless when they assume everyone knows what they know. They genuinely have not yet built the cognitive machinery to represent a false belief as false and act on it anyway. Theory of mind is, in a sense, the piece of the picture that finishes what Piaget started: it is one specific, testable form of moving beyond an egocentric, single-perspective view of the world, and it typically comes into place as children are transitioning out of the preoperational stage.

The classic test is the false-belief task, most famously the Sally-Anne task. A child watches a puppet show: Sally puts a marble in a basket and leaves the room. While she is gone, Anne moves the marble to a box. The child is asked, where will Sally look for her marble? Children younger than about four typically answer that Sally will look in the box, because that is where the marble actually is. They cannot yet separate what they themselves know from what Sally could possibly know, since she was not in the room to see the marble move. Around age four to five, most children start passing the task reliably, correctly predicting that Sally will look in the basket because that is where she believes it still is, even though the child watching knows that belief is now false. This shift is one of the most replicated findings in developmental psychology, and it appears across many cultures, though the exact age can shift somewhat depending on task wording and culture.

Theory of mind is not a switch that flips once and is done. Simpler precursors, like joint attention and understanding that people can want different things, show up in infancy and toddlerhood. More sophisticated forms, like understanding that someone can have a false belief about another person's belief, or appreciating sarcasm and white lies, continue developing into middle childhood and beyond. Theory of mind also matters well beyond the psychology classroom: it underlies everyday social skills like empathy, deception, persuasion, and cooperative play, and researchers have studied atypical theory of mind development, including in autism, as one lens for understanding social communication differences, though it is only one piece of a much larger and still-debated picture.
